title: Head injury: intubation (RSI)
stem: Resus 3. A 43-year-old roofer (about 75 kg) fell about 5 metres onto grass. He has facial injuries and blood coming from the left ear. HR 88, BP 136/74, RR 14, SpO2 93% on oxygen, GCS 9. The anaesthetist is 20 minutes away. You lead the team and will secure the airway.

phases.title: Prepare
phases.goal: The airway trolley, monitoring and the handover.

phases.title: Primary survey
phases.goal: Examine him yourself: why does he need a tube?

phases.title: Plan and drugs
phases.goal: Brief the team, then draw up the right drugs at the right doses.

phases.title: Intubate
phases.goal: Pre-oxygenate, MILS, induce, then intubate yourself and secure it.

phases.title: Neuroprotection
phases.goal: Set the ventilator yourself, then pressure, position, sedation and the blown pupil.

phases.title: Imaging and transfer
phases.goal: Images, the neurosurgeon, and hand over.

review.text: Premedication. Your notes give lignocaine, atropine and a defasciculating dose of rocuronium. None is used routinely in emergency RSI now. Fentanyl 1–3 microgram/kg is the usual adjunct in a normotensive head injury.
Cricoid pressure. Your script applies it routinely. DAS and many emergency services now make it optional, and it is released if it spoils the view.

Blood pressure target. Your notes give systolic over 90, the older ATLS figure. Current targets (Brain Trauma Foundation, ATLS): at least 110 mmHg for ages 15–49 and over 70, at least 100 mmHg for ages 50–69.

Ongoing sedation. Your script's propofol 50–200 microgram/kg/min (3–12 mg/kg/h) is above the usual 1–4 mg/kg/h, and diazepam is not used for sedation after intubation. Use propofol with fentanyl or morphine.

notes:
Checked against NICE NG232 (Head injury, 2023), ATLS 11th edition, Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition, and the Difficult Airway Society 2025 guideline and emergency airway checklists.

Indications to intubate after head injury (NICE): GCS 8 or less, loss of airway reflexes, ventilatory failure (PaO2 < 13 kPa on oxygen or PaCO2 > 6 kPa), spontaneous hyperventilation (PaCO2 < 4 kPa), irregular breathing, seizures, bleeding into the mouth, or agitation that prevents safe transfer. GCS 9 with a bleeding face and a falling saturation meets these criteria.

Drugs: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg (use less in shock) or etomidate; propofol at a reduced dose only if the pressure is good. Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg, or suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg. Fentanyl 1–3 microgram/kg blunts the pressor surge in a normotensive head injury. Your notes list lignocaine, atropine and a defasciculating dose of rocuronium as premedication; current emergency practice does not use them routinely, so they score nothing here.

Cricoid pressure: your script applies it routinely. DAS and many emergency services now make it optional and release it if it spoils the view. It is not scored either way.

After intubation: head up 30 degrees, SpO2 94–98%, PaCO2 4.5–5.0 kPa, and a systolic of at least 110 mmHg for ages 15–49 and over 70 (at least 100 mmHg for 50–69; BTF). Your notes give systolic > 90; that is the older ATLS figure. Ongoing sedation with propofol 1–4 mg/kg/h plus fentanyl or morphine; your script's 50–200 microgram/kg/min (3–12 mg/kg/h) is above the usual range, and diazepam is not used. Tape rather than ties so neck veins are not compressed. No steroids (CRASH). Hypertonic saline or mannitol only for signs of herniation; brief hyperventilation only as a bridge to surgery.

steps.label: Airway trolley
steps.hint: Prepare for a difficult airway: two suctions, videolaryngoscope, bougie, supraglottic airway, front-of-neck kit, capnography.

opts.t: Two working Yankauer suckers
Videolaryngoscope and a direct laryngoscope, bougie
Size 7.0 and 8.0 tubes, cuffs checked, syringe
Second-generation supraglottic airway (plan B)
Scalpel–bougie–tube front-of-neck kit (plan D)
Waveform capnography on the circuit
Nasopharyngeal airway for his blocked nose
opts.r: Blood from the ear and facial injuries: possible base of skull fracture. No nasal airways.

steps.label: Monitoring
steps.hint: Ask the nurse to put the patient on the monitor.

opts.t: Monitoring on: ECG, NIBP, SpO2 and capnography ready.
opts.mark: Asks for continuous ECG, NIBP and SpO2 monitoring

steps.label: Paramedic handover
steps.hint: Mechanism, injuries, signs (including the first GCS), treatment.

Mechanism.r: Fell off a roof, about 5 m, onto grass, 40 minutes ago.

Injuries.r: Facial swelling, blood from the left ear, a scalp laceration. Moving all limbs at scene.

Signs.r: GCS 13 at scene. Dropped to 9 in the ambulance. He vomited once.
Left pupil looked bigger in the last few minutes.

Treatment.r: Oxygen, collar and blocks, one 18 G. No drugs.

steps.label: Primary survey
steps.hint: Airway first: blood in the mouth. Then B, C, and a full D.

Airway.r: Blood pooling in the pharynx. Gurgling clears with suction but returns.
A second person holds the head; the collar front can open for laryngoscopy.

B C.r: Equal expansion and air entry, RR 14, no injuries.
HR 88, BP 136/74, warm peripheries, abdomen soft, pelvis not tender.

Disability.r: Eyes open to pressure (E2), inappropriate words (V3), withdraws from pressure (M4): GCS 9.
Disability.mark: GCS scored by component: E2 V3 M4

Disability.r: Left 5 mm, sluggish. Right 3 mm, brisk.

Exposure.r: Bruising behind the left ear (Battle's sign). Blood-stained fluid from the left ear. Periorbital bruising.
Exposure.mark: Recognises base of skull fracture signs

steps.label: Brief the team
steps.hint: Say why you are intubating, the plan A to D, roles, and read the checklist.

opts.t: Indication: GCS 9 and falling, blood in the airway, needs CT and transfer
Plan A videolaryngoscope with bougie, B supraglottic airway, C face mask, D scalpel–bougie–tube
opts.mark: States plans A to D aloud

opts.t: Roles: I intubate, Nurse Yip drugs, colleague holds MILS, one watches the monitor
Read the RSI checklist aloud
Wait for the anaesthetist before doing anything
opts.r: He is bleeding into his airway and his GCS is falling. Delaying twenty minutes is not safe.

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Induction for a head injury, a relaxant, a blunt to the pressor surge, a vasopressor ready.

opts.t: Ketamine 1.5 mg/kg (110 mg) IV
Ketamine 4 mg/kg (300 mg) IV
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (90 mg) IV
Rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg (45 mg) IV
opts.r: Too little for RSI: 1.2 mg/kg for fast intubating conditions.

opts.t: Fentanyl 2 microgram/kg (150 microgram) IV
opts.mark: Opioid to blunt the pressor response

opts.t: Fentanyl 10 microgram/kg (750 microgram) IV
Metaraminol 0.5–1 mg boluses drawn up

opts.r: No evidence it improves outcome; it is not part of current emergency RSI.
opts.t: Lignocaine 1.5 mg/kg IV premedication

opts.r: Steroids increase mortality after head injury (CRASH trial).
opts.t: Dexamethasone 8 mg IV

opts.r: A full propofol dose drops the pressure. Low pressure harms the injured brain.
opts.t: Propofol 2.5 mg/kg IV
Pre-oxygenate 3 minutes: non-rebreather plus nasal cannula at 15 L
Open the collar front; colleague holds in-line stabilisation
Give induction agent, then the relaxant; wait 45–60 seconds
opts.mark: Gives drugs in sequence and waits for relaxation

Airway.t: Intubate: laryngoscope, tube through the cords, cuff up, capnography
Airway.r: Tube through the cords, cuff up. Capnography: a square trace on every breath.

Airway.t: Confirm the tube by listening to the chest alone
Airway.r: Auscultation misses oesophageal tubes. No trace, wrong place: use waveform capnography.

opts.t: Secure with tape, not a tie round the neck
opts.mark: Secures without compressing the neck veins

steps.label: Ventilator
steps.hint: Set it yourself: PaCO2 4.5–5.0 kPa for a head injury.

opts.t: Set the ventilator
opts.performHint: Intubated, 75 kg, head injury. A controlled mode, 6–8 mL/kg, a rate for PaCO2 4.5–5.0, oxygen to 94–98%. START.
mark: Oxygen, PEEP and a pressure limit

steps.label: After the tube
steps.hint: Position, pressure, and what not to do.

opts.t: Head up 30 degrees, collar loosened or blocks and tape
opts.mark: Head up 30 degrees, no venous obstruction

opts.t: Keep systolic at 110 or more (age 15–49)
Hyperventilate to an ETCO2 of 3 kPa for the next few hours
opts.r: Prolonged hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischaemia. Only briefly, as a bridge to theatre.

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Sedation on the ventilator; an osmotic agent for the blown pupil.

opts.t: Propofol and fentanyl infusions: propofol 1–4 mg/kg/h with fentanyl
Propofol and fentanyl propofol 12 mg/kg/h
opts.r: Well above the usual 1–4 mg/kg/h: hypotension harms the injured brain.

opts.t: Hypertonic saline 3% 250 mL IV over 15 minutes
opts.mark: Treats signs of herniation with hyperosmolar therapy

opts.t: Hypertonic saline 3% 1 L IV stat

steps.label: Investigations
steps.hint: Tube position film, gas, then CT head and C-spine.

Bedside.r: Tube tip about 5 cm above the carina.
Bedside.mark: Checks tube position on a chest film

Bedside.t: Arterial gas after 10 minutes on the ventilator

CT.r: Left biconvex hyperdense collection under a temporal fracture, midline shift about 6 mm.
CT.mark: CT head and C-spine: left extradural haematoma with shift

steps.label: Phone
steps.hint: Neurosurgery for evacuation; transfer with a doctor who can manage the airway.

opts.t: Neurosurgeon: left EDH with shift and a dilated pupil — emergency evacuation
opts.mark: Refers to neurosurgery for emergency evacuation
opts.r: Neurosurgeon: Bring him straight to theatre. Keep the saline running.

opts.t: Transfer with an airway-trained doctor, full monitoring, drugs and a checklist
opts.mark: Safe transfer with an airway-competent escort

opts.t: Repeat CT in 6 hours to see if it grows
opts.r: An extradural with shift and a blown pupil needs theatre now.

steps.ask: The neurosurgical team is here. Please hand over.
steps.label: Handover
steps.hint: SBAR to the neurosurgeon or ICU.

opts.t: SBAR: 43, fall 5 m, GCS 13 → 9, left pupil blown, intubated at 10:52, left EDH with shift, 3% saline given, for theatre
opts.mark: Structured handover with GCS trend, times and plan
opts.r: The neurosurgical registrar takes him to theatre.

opts.t: Head injury, intubated, CT done
opts.r: No GCS trend, no pupils, no times, no plan.

qs.q: Which of these is a NICE indication to intubate after head injury?
qs.why: Also GCS 8 or less, loss of airway reflexes, ventilatory failure, hyperventilation, seizures, agitation preventing transfer.
wrong: A single seizure before arrival with full recovery

qs.q: Target PaCO2 after intubation for head injury?
wrong: Any value, as long as SpO2 is normal

qs.q: Why avoid a nasal airway in this man?
qs.why: Battle's sign and blood from the ear. A nasal tube or airway can pass into the cranial vault.

qs.q: Why tape rather than tie the tube?
qs.a: Ties compress the jugular veins and raise ICP
wrong: Tape is quicker to apply in the CT scanner
Ties can cause a cuff leak
Tape leaves no artefact on the CT images

rules.fail: To CT with an unprotected airway.

badge.name: Tube and Brain
badge.flavor: No trace, wrong place. Head up, CO2 normal, pressure up.

cards.q: After head injury, which PaCO2 range is the target?
cards.why: Normocapnia. Hypocapnia causes cerebral ischaemia; hypercapnia raises ICP.

cards.q: Minimum systolic for a 30-year-old with severe TBI (BTF)?
cards.why: BTF 4th: ≥110 for ages 15–49 and over 70, ≥100 for 50–69.

options: Auscultation of both axillae and the stomach
Misting inside the tube on expiration

cards.q: Which drug worsens mortality after head injury?
cards.why: The CRASH trial stopped steroids for head injury.
Mastoid bruising: a sign of base of skull fracture (with raccoon eyes, CSF leak, haemotympanum).
1.2 mg/kg gives intubating conditions in about 60 seconds.

cards.q: GCS motor score for withdrawal from a painful stimulus?
cards.why: M6 obeys, M5 localises, M4 normal flexion/withdrawal, M3 abnormal flexion, M2 extension, M1 none.
